Eating Insects

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Could insects be a viable source of nutrition for the world's growing human population?

Unique Selling Point:
It is estimated that the world's population will reach 9 billion by the year 2050, and we will have to more than double food production by then in order to feed everyone on earth. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has been actively promoting the eating of insects - Entomophagy - since 2003. In Africa many people are already eating insects, but not as a regular intake of protein, and of course in the West this is only now starting to become a reality. In America and Europe there are now some companies breeding crickets and other insects to produce protein powder as a meal supplement and even protein bars. Here in South Africa the times are also changing. Gourmet Grub is a company in Cape Town that produces ice cream from entomilk - cricket juice. Cape Town also has it's very own Insect Chef, who serves a variety of dishes made from one of the 1000+ edible insects available. In Johannesburg is our country's first cricket farm, where crickets are bred for consumption whole and as a protein powder nutritional supplement.

Summary:
The insert will start with Presenter in the kitchen with Gourmet Entomophagist, Zayaan Khan in her kitchen, cooking a delicious meal. But the ingredients are not ordinary. Instead of a beef fillet the viewer is presented with a variety of edible insects. Zayaan will speak about her love for insects, why it makes sense to eat insects and the different flavours and uses. Then we move on, saying it's not just isolated cases... more and more people are turning to insect eating as a healthy protein alternative. Endoki is a urban cricket farm in Johannesburg that breeds crickets for human consumption. Samantha Jack will speak about the nutritional value of insects, especially crickets. (She is a food scientist) and they will show us the process of breeding crickets all the way to getting the crickets ready for consumption. They will also speak to the environmental impacts of eating insects. Instead of 13 kg of vegetation to produce 1kg of beef protein, it now takes just over 1kg of vegetation to produce a kilogram of cricket protein. They also need much less water and do not emit methane or ammonia - pollutants associated with the beef industry.

Then we move to the FoodNext Africa Expo in Cape Town (28 & 29 Sept) where Gourmet Grub will be exhibiting their ice cream to the general public. They use larvae juice (entomilk) to make ice cream. So insects are not only for nutrition, but can also be enjoyed for their deliciousness. We speak to some of the general public at the Expo about their thoughts on Entomophagy and specifically the ice cream. We will also have an opportunity to interview Leah Bessa, the Head of Product Development who will explain how they "milk" black soldier fly larvae and where the idea came from. We will also film sections of the ice-cream making process.

The insert ends back in Zayaan's Kitchen. The meal is prepared and the presenter is ready to taste - Yummy!

Further information:
Solving the world's hunger and obesity problems is not easy, and the alternatives to beef fillets and cheese burgers need to be just as (if not more) delicious. Those who regularly eat insects will tell you that they have a range of flavours to suit everyone's tastes. The problem with eating insects is the perception we have of them -- most people view them as pests and that makes it "grillerig" to think of eating an insect.

Around 2 billion people regularly eat insects as part of their diet, and over 1,900 species are edible. The most commonly eaten bugs are beetles, caterpillars, bees, wasps, crickets and ants. However, as the world becomes westernised more people move away from eating insects and eat meat and other sources of protein. The problem is that we are simply too many people to sustain the current eating patterns of the West. So, by making insect eating more attractive we can increase our protein intake, optimise our health and save the planet at the same time. Insects are far more eco-friendly to breed than mammals bred for protein. Insects are packed with essential amino acids and micronutrients that could solve malnutrition problems amongst the poor. Insects are also rich in essential amino acids and omega-3 fatty acids; mealworms contain as much unsaturated omega-3 and six fatty acids as fish and even more than beef and pork. Some are also surprisingly high in iron; locusts contain up to 20 mg/100g iron and mopane caterpillars contain a mighty 31 mg/100g, whereas beef only contains around 6 mg/100g. Some insects are as much as 80% protein by weight. Insects are cold-blooded and thus require less energy to maintain their internal body temperature. This means they are very efficient at converting feed into edible body mass, unlike cattle. Crickets require around 2 kg of feed to produce 1 kg of meat, and around 80% is edible. Cattle, on the other hand, require 8 - 12 kg to produce the same amount of meat, but only 40% of the cow can be consumed.

Insects also require significantly less land and water than traditionally farmed animals and also reproduce much more quickly. They also have shorter life spans and thus can be grown quickly and farmed in large quantities in small areas. Insects produce a fraction of greenhouse gases such as methane and ammonia when compared with other livestock, particularly cattle. Furthermore, they can consume animal waste or plants that people and livestock cannot. There is also no need for antibiotics in the farming of insects.

Additionally, according to the FDA in the US, we've been eating insects for some time without thinking about it: Take beer for example—the acceptable limit of insect infestation in hops is 2,500 aphids per 10 grams. Canned fruit juices are allowed up to 1 maggot per 250 ml, curry powder is allowed up to 100 insect fragments (head, body, legs) per 25 grams and chopped dates are allowed up to 10 whole dead insects. The list goes on and on.

Globally there are an estimated 40 tonnes of insects per human, so we will probably not run out soon.

Script:


EATING INSECTS


V/O
With every passing second we, humans, need more resources to survive... To feed the planet, the UN estimates that food production will have to double by the year 2050....
LINK – Kitchen Steak
At the moment the world population increases by about 200,000 people per day. Already there are over 7.5 billion mouths to feed. The western diet of monoculture crops, overexploited fish and intensive meat farming is putting massive strain on the planet... so perhaps the time has come for us to think differently about food.
V/O
Entomophagy is the eating of insects and well-known entomophagist Zayaan Khan is an expert in the different tastes and flavours insects can offer.
Zayaan
I'll be making some.. just a Mopani Smoortjie, very quick and easy .
V/O
Globally about 2 billion people regularly eat insects, even here in South Africa.
Zayaan
If I go to a workshop or an event in the heart of Limpopo or in the Freestate or in the Eastern Cape, anywhere that's not so city and I say who here eats insects a lot of people will put up their hands but if I do that within Cape Town or in Joburg people are going to say no gross why? So as a nation we eat a lot of insects, as a continent…
V/O
Insects are rich in amino acids and often contain more than double the protein of more conventional meat.

They use up to 2000 times less water than cattle, and need very little space. They emit hardly any greenhouse gases and can be harvested in a matter of weeks.
Zayaan
In a country where there is so much meat consumption it is good to diversify in that space.

V/O
Entomologist, Prof Eerik Holim agrees that eating insects is a good idea.
Prof Holm
In every sense these insects are a bargain.The problem is they're too small to make it worthwhile to go and hunt them. I mean insect eaters are small animals. Except things like Aarvark and so on which go for big colonies. And that's why all the indigenous peoples in Africa concentrated on things like termites, which you can harvest in big quantities when they fly out, locusts which come over in big swarms, and then these mopane worms which come in outbreaks where you can really harvest kilograms in a day – then it's worthwhile.
V/O
Farming insects specifically for consumption means that they can be harvested in larger quantities, making it more viable as a food source for humans.
V/O
In this suburban backyard it's not just the chickens that eat well... Elvis Rashirai, farms insects for his own consumption, and hopes expand his farm for mass production in the future ..
ELVIS
CLAIRE: So what do we have here, Elvis?

What I have here are actually crickets in different stages. So in this box here there's creatures in here. So they like hiding. This is their feed. What we have here is grain and a little bit of wheat in there. And also some carrots. As you can see they love carrots. And usually crickets, I say they are as good as what you feed them.

V/O:
Besides the crickets, Elvis also farms mealworms.
Elvis
Claire: So how would you prepare meal worms?

So, mealworms, basically what I'll do is, if I want to prepare them I'll isolate them for 2 to three days and that way they clean themselves out and after that I just actually put them in the fridge to just quieten them down a little bit so at least they don't move around when I cook them.
Link
When it comes to eating insects you are spoiled for choice because there are over 2000 edible insects.
Zayaan
If you're wanting to serve a delicious meal then yes, your easiest go-to is going to be mopane worms. If you want to be a little bit different you could – things like escargot, like snails that's a very common insect and that you'll find in restaurants. What I ended up doing was having to look for things like ant eggs to look for other kinds of insects that are edible.


LINK
Most of us get the heeby-jeebies at just the thought of eating insects but it's all about perception because we don't even think twice that prawns mussels and oysters are a regular feature on our dinner tables.
Prof Holm
The funny thing is we will eat crayfish and krill, which are much more horrible, looking anyway, and also their diet is much more horrible than an insect that eats leaves like a grasshopper. They are scavengers, they are hyenas of the sea, but we have no problem eating them because somehow it's in our culture.
ELVIS
I know a lot of people freak when they see a cricket and think ai, it's creepy, I can't eat it. But there's actually many ways of actually eating them.
V/O
Of course the idea of eating insects is easier to digest when disguised as something delicious, … like ice cream. But this is not just regular dairy ice cream with cricket powder added, the actual milk is derived from black soldier fly larvae.
Leah
We basically take the whole insect and process them into what we call the diary alternative. So, there's no milking involved specifically. It's basically just a milk in its application.
V/O
Food scientist Leah Bessa and her team, with assistance from the Cape Peninsula University of Technology, and Technology Innovation Agency have developed “entomilk” which is pasteurised and 100% foodsafe, … and they're introducing it to the public as ice cream in 3 different flavours.
VOX POPS
And it's made out of? Insects. Okay. Really, really? It's made out of insects? It's good.


1, 2, 3 It's really good! Hmm ja, not bad.

Dark chocolate is amazing! Taste good. Ja That's my choice. Dark Chocolate.
V/O
Amazingly a kilogram of larvae delivers a litre of entomilk, and the team is confident that once mass production starts it will be a cost- comparative viable dairy alternative.
Leah
I think a lot of people are apprehensive because it's not something you usually eat, especially in the western world but you know there's a lot of health benefits and it's high in protein and fat, and your minerals, zinc iron and calcium. And it's also incredibly sustainable to farm them. In a world where agriculture can't keep up with the growing demand for food we are going to have to look for alternatives.
V/O
But people are not necessarily going to change their perceptions if the end product is not palatable.
Claire on Camera
So you say chocolate is your favourite... That's peanut butter yummy deliciousness in my mouth right now. I wouldn't have known once upon a time when this ice-cream was a baby it was this....
Zayaan
Insects are delicious and there's a whole new world that you can discover with your culinary instincts and just in terms of tastes.


Claire & Zayaan
C:I think it's time to have some mopane worms. How do you suggest, can I just take one?

Z:Go ahead, take one, and also use the bread and dip the bread into...

C:I'm Going to have one. Go Mopane worms! You know a Mopane worm is substantial.

Z:It's very substantial.

C:Crunchy, earthy, meaty...

Z:Smokey... very meaty.

C:Very meaty






PROMO 10”
With the human population exploding, time has come for us to think differently about food. Insects are easy to farm, have a small eco footprint and are packed with proteins...


PROMO 15”
Eating insects is not only good for the planet, they're also packed with nutrients and fibre.

UPSOUND ZAYAAN:
Insects are delicious and there's a whole new world that you can discover with your culinary instincts and just in terms of tastes.

Is it time to swap steak for crickets?


PROMO 15”
The thought of eating crickets makes many a stomach churn, yet we don't think twice about eating crayfish and prawns.

UPSOUND PROF HOLM:
They are hyenas of the sea, but we have no problem eating them because somehow it's in our culture.



PROMO 30”
There are about 2 billion people on earth who regularly eat insects, but how do you feel about swapping your steak for Mopane worms or even crickets?

UPSOUND Elvis:
I know a lot of people freak when they see a cricket and think ai, it's creepy, I can't eat it.

Insects are becoming a real, viable meat alternative that is both kinder to the planet and nutritions.

UPSOUND ZAYAAN:
Insects are delicious and there's a whole new world that you can discover with your culinary instincts and just in terms of tastes.





If you’re keen to incorporate insects in your diet, there is even a range of recipe books on the market to help you prepare the insects of your choice.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Could insects be a viable source of nutrition for the world's growing human population?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: It is estimated that the world's population will reach 9 billion by the year 2050, and we will have to more than double food production by then in order to feed everyone on earth. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has been actively promoting the eating of insects - Entomophagy - since 2003. In Africa many people are already eating insects, but not as a regular intake of protein, and of course in the West this is only now starting to become a reality. In America and Europe there are now some companies breeding crickets and other insects to produce protein powder as a meal supplement and even protein bars. Here in South Africa the times are also changing. Gourmet Grub is a company in Cape Town that produces ice cream from entomilk - cricket juice. Cape Town also has it's very own Insect Chef, who serves a variety of dishes made from one of the 1000+ edible insects available. In Johannesburg is our country's first cricket farm, where crickets are bred for consumption whole and as a protein powder nutritional supplement.
metadata.Summary: The insert will start with Presenter in the kitchen with Gourmet Entomophagist, Zayaan Khan in her kitchen, cooking a delicious meal. But the ingredients are not ordinary. Instead of a beef fillet the viewer is presented with a variety of edible insects. Zayaan will speak about her love for insects, why it makes sense to eat insects and the different flavours and uses. Then we move on, saying it's not just isolated cases... more and more people are turning to insect eating as a healthy protein alternative. Endoki is a urban cricket farm in Johannesburg that breeds crickets for human consumption. Samantha Jack will speak about the nutritional value of insects, especially crickets. (She is a food scientist) and they will show us the process of breeding crickets all the way to getting the crickets ready for consumption. They will also speak to the environmental impacts of eating insects. Instead of 13 kg of vegetation to produce 1kg of beef protein, it now takes just over 1kg of vegetation to produce a kilogram of cricket protein. They also need much less water and do not emit methane or ammonia - pollutants associated with the beef industry. Then we move to the FoodNext Africa Expo in Cape Town (28 & 29 Sept) where Gourmet Grub will be exhibiting their ice cream to the general public. They use larvae juice (entomilk) to make ice cream. So insects are not only for nutrition, but can also be enjoyed for their deliciousness. We speak to some of the general public at the Expo about their thoughts on Entomophagy and specifically the ice cream. We will also have an opportunity to interview Leah Bessa, the Head of Product Development who will explain how they "milk" black soldier fly larvae and where the idea came from. We will also film sections of the ice-cream making process. The insert ends back in Zayaan's Kitchen. The meal is prepared and the presenter is ready to taste - Yummy!
metadata.Further information: Solving the world's hunger and obesity problems is not easy, and the alternatives to beef fillets and cheese burgers need to be just as (if not more) delicious. Those who regularly eat insects will tell you that they have a range of flavours to suit everyone's tastes. The problem with eating insects is the perception we have of them -- most people view them as pests and that makes it "grillerig" to think of eating an insect. Around 2 billion people regularly eat insects as part of their diet, and over 1,900 species are edible. The most commonly eaten bugs are beetles, caterpillars, bees, wasps, crickets and ants. However, as the world becomes westernised more people move away from eating insects and eat meat and other sources of protein. The problem is that we are simply too many people to sustain the current eating patterns of the West. So, by making insect eating more attractive we can increase our protein intake, optimise our health and save the planet at the same time. Insects are far more eco-friendly to breed than mammals bred for protein. Insects are packed with essential amino acids and micronutrients that could solve malnutrition problems amongst the poor. Insects are also rich in essential amino acids and omega-3 fatty acids; mealworms contain as much unsaturated omega-3 and six fatty acids as fish and even more than beef and pork. Some are also surprisingly high in iron; locusts contain up to 20 mg/100g iron and mopane caterpillars contain a mighty 31 mg/100g, whereas beef only contains around 6 mg/100g. Some insects are as much as 80% protein by weight. Insects are cold-blooded and thus require less energy to maintain their internal body temperature. This means they are very efficient at converting feed into edible body mass, unlike cattle. Crickets require around 2 kg of feed to produce 1 kg of meat, and around 80% is edible. Cattle, on the other hand, require 8 - 12 kg to produce the same amount of meat, but only 40% of the cow can be consumed. Insects also require significantly less land and water than traditionally farmed animals and also reproduce much more quickly. They also have shorter life spans and thus can be grown quickly and farmed in large quantities in small areas. Insects produce a fraction of greenhouse gases such as methane and ammonia when compared with other livestock, particularly cattle. Furthermore, they can consume animal waste or plants that people and livestock cannot. There is also no need for antibiotics in the farming of insects. Additionally, according to the FDA in the US, we've been eating insects for some time without thinking about it: Take beer for example—the acceptable limit of insect infestation in hops is 2,500 aphids per 10 grams. Canned fruit juices are allowed up to 1 maggot per 250 ml, curry powder is allowed up to 100 insect fragments (head, body, legs) per 25 grams and chopped dates are allowed up to 10 whole dead insects. The list goes on and on. Globally there are an estimated 40 tonnes of insects per human, so we will probably not run out soon.
